name: Bioconductor_search_packages
description: Search Bioconductor bioinformatics R packages by keyword or analysis type. Results use exact r-universe skip pagination: start with offset=0 and continue with metadata.next_offset while metadata.has_more is true; metadata.total_results is exact. Returns matching packages with title, description, usage count, and relevance score.

q.description: Search query for Bioconductor packages. Can be a keyword, analysis type, or topic. Examples: 'differential expression', 'single cell RNA', 'proteomics', 'ChIP-seq', 'methylation', 'variant calling', 'gene set enrichment', 'phylogenetics', 'metabolomics', 'flow cytometry'

offset.description: Zero-based package offset. Continue with metadata.next_offset while metadata.has_more is true.

Package.description: Package name (use with Bioconductor_get_package for details)

_usedby.description: Number of other packages that depend on this one (popularity indicator)

updated.description: Last update timestamp (string or Unix epoch integer)

_id.description: The search index's internal document id, e.g. '6ae75cf12e87f76f20acd09a'. Not the package name and not stable across reindexing.

_searchresults.description: How many packages matched the query in total, e.g. 46, repeated on every row. The returned list is only a page of them, and this is the only field that says so.

_user.description: Owner of the search index the hit came from, e.g. 'bioc'.

_uuid.description: The index's numeric uuid for the document.

match.description: Raw text-match score for the hit, e.g. 115.09784574086044.

rank.description: The combined ranking score results are ordered by, e.g. 949.2221839842782. Blends the text match with popularity, so it is not comparable to 'match' and is what actually decided the order.

stars.description: How many GitHub stars the package's repository has, e.g. 12.

name: Bioconductor_get_package
description: Get detailed metadata for a specific Bioconductor R package by name. Returns comprehensive information including version, description, dependencies, biocViews categories, author/maintainer, license, download statistics, GitHub stars, reverse dependencies (packages that use it), and git repository URL. Useful for evaluating packages before installation or for understanding the Bioconductor ecosystem. Use Bioconductor_search_packages first to find package names.

_downloads.description: Download statistics with count and source URL

_usedby.description: Number of reverse dependencies (packages using this one)

_dependencies.description: List of dependency objects with package name, version, and role (Depends/Imports/Suggests)

_id.description: The search index's internal document id, e.g. '6ae75cf12e87f76f20acd09a'. Not the package name and not stable across reindexing.

_searchresults.description: How many packages matched the query in total, e.g. 46, repeated on every row. The returned list is only a page of them, and this is the only field that says so.

_user.description: Owner of the search index the hit came from, e.g. 'bioc'.

Authors@R.description: The package's authors as an R expression, e.g. 'c(person("Michael", "Love", email=..., role=c("aut","cre")), ...)'. Roles are in here and nowhere else, so this is what says who to cite ('aut') as against who to email ('cre'). NOTE the '@' in the property name.

Config/pak/sysreqs.description: System libraries the package needs, e.g. 'zlib1g-dev'. An install fails on a machine without them, and nothing else in the record warns of it. NOTE the '/' characters in the property name.

Date/Publication.description: When the build was published, e.g. '2026-10-30 14:15:37 UTC'. NOTE the '/' in the property name.

Encoding.description: Character encoding the package's files use, e.g. 'UTF-8'. Reading a non-UTF-8 package's help text as UTF-8 mangles author names.

Packaged.description: When and by whom the tarball was built, as 'Date' and 'User'.

RemoteRef.description: Git ref the build came from, e.g. 'HEAD'.

RemoteSha.description: Exact commit the build came from, e.g. '4ba3e3a159da872566d825609a119a7615069663'. The only field that pins the source to a revision; a version number does not.

Repository.description: The repository serving this build, e.g. 'https://bioc.r-universe.dev'. Which of several mirrors the metadata describes.

RoxygenNote.description: Which roxygen2 version generated the documentation, e.g. '7.3.3'.

VignetteBuilder.description: Packages needed to build the vignettes, e.g. 'knitr, rmarkdown'. A comma-delimited string, not a list.

_abi.description: The package's binary interface, as 'exports' and 'imports'. What breaks downstream if this package changes.

_assets.description: Extra files published beside the artefact, e.g. ['extra/citation.cff', ...]. citation.cff is the machine-readable citation.

_binaries.description: Built binaries, each with its R version, OS and package version, e.g. {'r': '4.7.0', 'os': 'linux', 'version': '1.53.7'}. Whether a binary exists for the caller's R and platform, as against having to build from source.

_bioc.description: Bioconductor release lines carrying the package, each with 'branch' ('devel' or 'release'), its 'version' and the 'bioc' release number, e.g. {'branch': 'devel', 'version': '1.53.6', 'bioc': '3.24'}. The devel and release versions differ, and this is the only field that says which is which.

_bioccheck.description: BiocCheck results as counts of 'error', 'warning' and 'note'. Bioconductor's own quality gate; a package can build cleanly and still carry BiocCheck errors.

_buildurl.description: The CI run that produced the build, e.g. a github.com/r-universe/bioc/actions/runs URL. Where to read the build log when _status is not 'success'.

_commit.description: The source commit, with its id, author, committer, message and time. The change this build contains.

_contributors.description: Everyone who has committed to the package, each with their login, commit count and uuid, e.g. {'user': 'mikelove', 'count': 831}. Who actually maintains it, as distinct from who is named in Authors@R.

_cranurl.description: The package's CRAN URL, or the BOOLEAN false when it is not on CRAN - measured false for DESeq2. A field that is sometimes a URL and sometimes a boolean.

_created.description: When the artefact was created, e.g. '2026-11-01T12:52:44.000Z'.

_devurl.description: The package's development repository, e.g. 'https://github.com/thelovelab/deseq2'. The place to file an issue; _upstream is only the Bioconductor mirror.

_distro.description: The Linux distribution the build ran on, e.g. 'resolute'.

_expires.description: When r-universe will stop serving this build, e.g. '2027-02-09T13:16:47.000Z'. A pinned URL stops working after it, which nothing else warns of.

_exports.description: Every object the package exports, e.g. ['collapseReplicates', ...] - 57 for DESeq2. What a caller can actually use without knowing the package.

_fileid.description: Content-addressed download URL for the artefact.

_filesize.description: Size of the artefact in bytes, e.g. 3025259.

_help.description: The package's help pages, each with its 'page' and 'title' - 40 for DESeq2. The documentation index, without which a caller has to guess function names.

_indexed.description: True when the build is in the package index, so install.packages can see it. An unindexed build exists and cannot be installed.

_jobs.description: The individual build jobs, each with its id, duration and config, e.g. {'job': 125159223001, 'time': 230, 'config': 'bioc-check'}. Which checks ran and how long they took.

_maintainer.description: The maintainer's name, email, login, description and uuid. Who to contact; Authors@R gives the role but not the resolved account.

_mentions.description: How many times the package is mentioned in the literature r-universe indexes, e.g. 9583. The usage signal; download counts are not in this record.

_nocasepkg.description: The package name lower-cased, e.g. 'deseq2'. What r-universe matches case-insensitively against.

_owner.description: The r-universe that owns this build, e.g. 'bioc'.

_published.description: When it was published to the universe.

_rbuild.description: R version used to build the source tarball, e.g. '4.6.2'.

_realowner.description: The underlying owner where _owner is an alias.

_registered.description: True when the package is registered in the universe rather than only built there.

_rundeps.description: Every package needed at run time, e.g. ['abind', ...] - 45 for DESeq2. The real install cost, which the DESCRIPTION's direct Imports understates.

_selfowned.description: True when the package is built in its own author's universe rather than a mirror universe.

_sha256.description: SHA-256 of the artefact, e.g. '85b66c89e43a1a9a4dcd...'. What verifies a download; the version string does not.

_status.description: Build outcome, e.g. 'success' or 'failure'. A record with a failed status still carries version and metadata, so nothing else reveals there is no installable artefact.

_sysdeps.description: System libraries the binary links against, each with its shlib and system package, e.g. {'shlib': 'liblapack', 'package': 'libopenblas0-pthread'}. Why a binary built elsewhere may not load here.

_topics.description: Topic tags for the package, e.g. ['sequencing', ...] - 14 for DESeq2.

_type.description: What kind of artefact this record is for, e.g. 'src' or 'win'/'mac' for a binary.

_universes.description: Every r-universe this package appears in, e.g. ['bioc', ...]. The same package can be served by several, and each may hold a different version.

_updates.description: Commit activity by week, each {week, n}, e.g. {'week': '2025-44', 'n': 2}. Whether the package is still being worked on.

_upstream.description: The git repository r-universe builds from, e.g. 'https://github.com/bioc/DESeq2'. Where the built artefact actually came from, which can differ from the project's own home.

_userbio.description: The owning account's profile - uuid, type, name, followers and description. Whether the publisher is a person or an organisation.

_vignettes.description: The package's vignettes, each with its source, built filename and title. The worked examples, which are usually the only usable introduction.
